entries.title: Trump says Board of Peace agrees on Hamas disarming
entries.summary: The US president hailed the "historic" agreement on Hamas' disarmament as a "major milestone" in implementing his 20-point plan to end the conflict in Gaza and rebuild the Palestinian enclave. DW has more.
entries.content:
Middle East

Trump says Board of Peace agrees on Hamas disarming

Published July 31, 2026last updated July 31, 2026

The US president hailed the "historic" agreement on Hamas' disarmament as a "major milestone" in implementing his 20-point plan to end the conflict in Gaza and rebuild the Palestinian enclave. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Donald Trump says his Board of Peacehas reached a 'historic' agreement on Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups in theGaza Stripdisarming
  • The US president says the step is a 'major milestone' in implementing his 20-point plan for Gaza
  • The announcement comes after negotiators from mediating nations Egypt, Qatar and Turkey met in Cairo on Thursday to discuss Hamas' disarmament
  • Hamasofficials reportedly confirm the group has agreed to the Board of Peace's plan
  • Israelhas yet to comment

Here is a roundup of the main developments of the conflict in Iran and the Middle East on Friday, July 31 2026:

Skip next section IN DEPTH — Palestinians in Gaza: Stuck between Hamas and Israel

IN DEPTH — Palestinians in Gaza: Stuck between Hamas and Israel

Hamas is planning to transfer control of Gaza's civilian administration to Palestinian technocrats as part of the fragile US ceasefire. How is that affecting the daily lives of people living in Gaza?

Learn more about how the transition of power in the Gaza Strip will affect Palestinian civilians in this report.

Skip next section What has Israel said about the plans?

What has Israel said about the plans?

Israel has not commented since Donald Trump announced that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement with Hamas on the militant group's disarmament.

But before Trump's announcement late on Thursday, an Israeli official had said a 15-point proposal that was being discussed by officials from mediators Egypt, Qatar and Turkey did not meet Israel's demands for the complete demilitarization of the Gaza Strip.

Hamas has said its disarmament hinges on Israeli troops completely withdrawing from the enclave.

Israel, on the other hand, insists that it will not withdraw beyond the so-called "yellow line" before Hamas has completely disarmed.

Skip next section What will happen to Hamas' weapons?

What will happen to Hamas' weapons?

Under the agreement with the Board of Peace to disarm Hamas, a transitional Palestinian committee of technocrats will run Gaza and will oversee the storing of the militant group's weapons, a senior Hamas official told the AFP news agency.

Hamas would hand over its arms to that transitional administration and to international mediators, rather than Israel.

"The National Committee for Administration of Gaza (NCAG) shall manage and execute the cataloguing and storage of weapons in accordance with the agreed timetable," the official said.

"The National Committee will be the sole entity authorised to retain, store, or control weapons in Gaza," they added.

Skip next section What is in Trump's 20-point peace plan for Gaza?

What is in Trump's 20-point peace plan for Gaza?

Donald Trump says the agreement on Hamas disarming is a "major milestone" in his 20-point plan for post-war Gaza.

The plan was unveiled in September last year.

Here's a reminder of some of the plan's main aims:

  • Creating a pathway to a Palestinian state, which Israel has consistently and vehemently opposed
  • Removing Hamas from power and securing a commitment from the militant group to disarm
  • Reforming the Palestinian Authority, which runs the occupied West Bank
  • Providing an economic plan for Gaza's post-war recovery and growth
  • Providing security guarantees for Gaza, which would be enforced by the US and regional powers
  • Ensuring that Israel halts all operations immediately upon an agreement, hands over any captured territories, and pledges not to occupy or annex Gaza
  • The plan had also called for the return of remaining Israeli hostages, in exchange for Palestinian prisoners
  • Those steps were fulfilled before the  first phase of a ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas

DW spoke to Palestinian-American humanitarian activist Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib in October about the prospects of Hamas fully disarming. Here's what he had to say:

In the wake of Hamas' announcement on Friday, Alkhatib cautioned that the militant group's claims should be "treated with firm skepticism."

In a post on X, he said a Palestinian police force and a transitional government in Gaza is still "many months away," which will give the group "ample time" to shore up contingency plans and preserve its influence on the enclave's population.

"Just as there is no olive oil without olives, there is no Hamas without weapons and armed resistance. Some members may genuinely want to evolve and enter a political process, and they may; but they are unlikely to do so sustainably and successfully while still operating under the Hamas banner and identity," Alkhatib explained.

Skip next section Hamas officials confirm deal to end conflict with Israel

Hamas officials confirm deal to end conflict with Israel

Senior officials from Palestinian militant group Hamas have confirmed that they have agreed a deal to end the conflict with Israel.

The confirmation comes after US President Donald Trump announced late Thursday night that the Board of Peace had agreed on the militant group's disarmament.

Speaking to the AFP news agency on condition of anonymity early Friday, two officials confirmed that they had come to an agreement.

They also said they expect mediators Egypt, Qatar and Turkey to make sure Israel fulfills its part of the deal, including the "gradual withdrawal" of Israeli troops from the enclave.

Israel has yet to comment on the announcements by Trump or by Hamas.

Skip next section Trump: Board of Peace reaches deal over Hamas disarmament

Trump: Board of Peace reaches deal over Hamas disarmament

US President Donald Trump has said that the Board of Peace has reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas, as well as other Palestinian militant groups in Gaza.

In a post on his Truth Social platform, Trump said the "historic" deal is a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security."

"This agreement is a critical step towards Gaza finally being governed by a new Palestinian government that will work closely with the Board of Peace to help the Palestinian people. At the same time, Israel will have the security it deserves, with Gaza no longer used as a base for terror attacks," the US president said.

Trump said the deal represented a "major milestone" in implementing his 20-Point Plan to end the conflict in Gaza and rebuild the war-torn enclave.

The US president explained that the agreement would be carried out in "carefully structured phases".

"As disarmament is completed, Israeli forces will withdraw, and the International Stabilization Force will work with a new Palestinian police force to take responsibility for Gaza being safe for its residents and its neighbors," he said.

Trump announced the agreement the day after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu returned to Israel from a visit to the US, during which he met with the US leader at the White House.

The US president also thanked mediators Egypt, Qatar, and Turkey for making "this historic breakthrough possible."

Earlier on Thursday, DW reported that negotiators meeting in Cairo had agreed on a 15-point roadmap on Hamas' disarmament, although amendments to the proposal were still being made.

While Trump has touted an agreement, there has been no official confirmation from Israel or from any of the mediators, Egypt, Qatar and Turkey.

Hamas has been designated a terrorist organization by Germany, the EU, the US and some Arab states.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

US President Donald Trump has announced what he is calling a "historic agreement" by his Board of Peace over the disarmament of Hamas and other Palestinian militant groups in the Gaza Strip.

The US leader says the deal, reached after negotiations with mediators Egypt, Qatar and Turkey, will see the withdrawal of Israeli troops from the enclave and a new Palestinian government and police force set up.

Stay tuned as we bring you more on this story and the other major developments from the Middle East.

To catch up on Thursday's news from the region, head over to our blog.

entries.title: Are Iran and Ukraine wars getting tangled in Caspian Sea?
entries.summary: Tehran has threatened a response after a Ukrainian strike on an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea that Kyiv says was carrying weapons to Russia. Still, Ukraine says it wants to avoid escalation with Tehran.
entries.content:
Asia

Are Iran and Ukraine wars getting tangled in Caspian Sea?

July 30, 2026

Tehran has threatened a response after a Ukrainian strike on an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea that Kyiv says was carrying weapons to Russia. Still, Ukraine says it wants to avoid escalation with Tehran.

A recent Ukrainian strike on an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea has drawn concerns that Russia's war in Ukraine and the war in Iran are becoming entangled.

Ukraine has said the ship was carrying military equipment from Iran to Russia. Iranian state media, citing Iran's ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, reported that the cargo vessel "Anna" was anchored approximately 5 kilometers (3 miles) from the entrance of the Volga River when it was attacked by drones causing an explosion. One sailor was reported killed.

Iran summoned Ukraine's charge d'affaires and described the incident as an act of aggression.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, said Ukrainian forces had carried out successful long-range strikes against a Russian warship and vessels that Kyiv says were transporting military cargo.

Ukraine has long accused Iran of helping Russia wage war through the supply and development of Iranian-designed drones.

Tehran has acknowledged earlier drone sales to Moscow but has rejected accusations that it supplied weapons specifically for use in the Ukraine war.

However, the Ukrainian military has extensive documented physical evidence that Iranian-designed Shahed drones have been deployed throughout the war that has dragged on for more than four years.

In March 2026, Russia launched nearly 950 Shahed, Gerber and other types of attack drones at Ukraine in a 24-hour period, according to Ukraine's Air Force.

Iran's Foreign Ministry has accused Ukraine of attempting to expand the geographical scope of its war with Russia. Kyiv, by contrast, presents its attacks in the Caspian Sea as part of an effort to disrupt military logistics supporting Moscow.

Will Iran strike Ukraine?

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a statement the attack "cannot go unanswered."

However, Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, told DW that Tehran is unlikely to respond immediately with a direct military strike against Ukraine.

"I believe the Islamic Republic will avoid an emotional reaction and choose a diplomatic response instead of a military one," he said, pointing to Tehran's summoning of the Ukrainian diplomat and the possibility of raising the matter at the UN Security Council.

On Monday, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha posted on X that Iran's accusations were "unjustified and groundless."

"The regime in Tehran is a direct accomplice to Russian aggression against Ukraine, fueling Moscow's criminal war with weapons that have killed Ukrainians since 2022," he wrote.

A day later, in a call with Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, Sybiha softened his tone and said that Ukraine wants to avoid unnecessary escalation with Iran.

Ukrainian Middle East expert Ihor Semyvolos considers the likelihood of an Iranian retaliatory attack on Ukraine to be very low.

"Attacks on ships or ports in the Caspian Sea are one thing, since this is related to Russia," which attacked Ukraine.

"However, an Iranian missile attack on Ukrainian territory is an entirely different matter. That would be a direct act of war," said Semyvolos, adding that such an attack "would only complicate the situation for Iran."

Austrian military expert Markus Reisner told DW that an Iranian missile attack on Ukraine is unlikely, even though Tehran possesses medium-range missiles.

Reisner said it would make little sense for Iran to actually launch a missile at a target on Ukrainian territory when there could be more important or higher-value targets elsewhere.

No 'new front' in Iran war

Reisner, currently head of research at Austria's Theresian Military Academy, added that the attack in the Caspian Sea does not indicate that Ukraine is now a participant in the Iran war.

Reisner points out that the Ukrainian military has been increasing attacks on maritime facilities, particularly in the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea, since May. Around 200 Russian ships, tankers and tugboats have already been hit.

Ukraine's goal is not "to open a new front against Iran, but rather to disrupt supply routes between Iran and Russia in the Caspian Sea as well," said Reisner.

Moscow-based analyst Vakhshiteh said, however, that the attack "can be seen as a signal and an indication that the geography of the Ukrainian war is expanding from the Black Sea to the Caspian Sea."

Ukrainian Middle East expert Ihor Semyvolos agrees. He finds it logical that Ukraine would expand its strategy to control sea lanes for arms deliveries and attempt to impose a general economic naval blockade against Russia in the south.

Ukrainian coordination with the US?

There is no direct evidence that the operation in the Caspian Sea was coordinated with the US, and the issue has not been publicly discussed, Semyvolos said.

"But it's obvious that Ukraine uses American intelligence data. Therefore, the Americans were most likely aware of it," Semyvolos believes.

Austrian military analyst Reisner emphasizes that the timing of Ukraine's attack plays a crucial role.

"Zelenskyy wants to clearly demonstrate here that Kyiv and Washington share a common enemy in Iran," Reisner said.

The Ukrainian attack could also be seen as a demonstration from Kyiv that it is actually a better ally in fighting Iran than some NATO countries, he added.

Zelenskyy met with US President Donald Trump in Washington this week, as ties between Kyiv and the Trump administration have turned positive along with Ukraine's advances on the battlefield.

Will Ukraine's Caspian Sea attacks continue?

As Ukrainian Foreign Minister Sybiha's statement on X indicates, Kyiv increasingly sees Iran and Russia as part of the same military ecosystem.

And Ukraine has also demonstrated tactical momentum in carrying out long-range drone strikes deep inside Russian territory.

Ukrainian analyst Semyvolos expects Ukraine to continue its operations in the Caspian Sea. He explains the timing of the operation by noting that the Ukrainian military now has the technical ability to carry out long-range strikes.

However, if Ukraine again targets Iranian vessels, Tehran faces an uncomfortable strategic choice.

Moscow-based analyst Vakhshiteh argues that a direct Iranian military response against Ukrainian territory risks creating a new front at a time when Tehran is already confronting attacks now concentrated in southern Iran.

Vakhshiteh also suggested that Iran could instead look for indirect ways to impose costs on Ukraine, including measures against shipping connected to Ukrainian interests.

However, such options would carry their own considerable escalation risks and there is no indication that Tehran has decided to pursue them.

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Spain will send troops to Ceuta to help with border security
entries.summary: Authorities in the Spanish city of Ceuta asked Madrid to declare a national emergency and send military assistance. Crowds of people breached the border of the territory next to Morocco as police lost control.
entries.content:
Published July 30, 2026last updated July 30, 2026

Authorities in the Spanish city of Ceuta asked Madrid to declare a national emergency and send military assistance. Crowds of people breached the border of the territory next to Morocco as police lost control.

Officials in the Spanish territory of Ceuta on the northwestern tip of Africa on Thursday asked the government in Madrid to declare a national emergency and send the army to help secure its border with Morocco. 

The call came as video footage showed crowds of people trying to walk around the breakwaters separating Moroccan and Spanish territory or otherwise scale the border fence. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez pledged an "immediate response."

Spain's Interior Ministry said later on Thursday that its armed forces would send personnel to Ceuta to support the border guards.

"The Armed Forces will reinforce the Guardia Civil in the exercise of its powers and any others that may be necessary to maintain civil security in the city of Ceuta," the ministry said.

What had happened in Ceuta during the day?

The Guardia Civil said that crowds broke through the fences into Spain after overwhelming police at the city's breakwater. Video footage showed hundreds swimming across from the Moroccan side, using inflatable inner tubes and other flotation aids.

"The situation is absolute chaos," Rachid Sbihi, head of the association that represents Spain's Guardia Civil in Ceuta, told the Associated Press. "It's not possible to give precise numbers but there are thousands of migrants crossing," he said, adding that the border had "totally collapsed."

The AFP news agency cited a spokesperson for the Spanish government's delegation in Ceuta as saying that nine people had died amid the offshore rush.

The scenes were reminiscent of a similar flashpoint at the border crossing in May of 2021 when more than 8,000 people entered the territory in just two days. 

In recent days, rescue parties had already noted increased numbers of people trying to swim around the border checks. 

What did the regional government say?

Juan Jesus Vivas, head of the Ceuta regional government, called for the Spanish government in Madrid to declare an emergency on grounds of national security, asking for more police and for the army to be deployed on the border. This followed a meeting of the city's board of spokespeople, who reached a unanimous agreement.

"Yesterday, I spoke out to warn of the extreme gravity of the migration crisis we are enduring," Vivas wrote online. "Today, mere hours later, the situation is even more critical: another night of mass arrivals, nearly a thousand people waiting outside the CETI [Temporary Migrant Reception Center], our reseources completely overwhelmed, and another life lost at sea."

He said that the small city was facing "a humanitarian and social emergency" of national proportions.

"We cannot face this pressure alone — pressure that has resulted in the arrival of between 1,500 and 2,000 people in just 10 days, equivalent to 2% of our population."

He wrote that "with every passing hour, the situation becomes more difficult" in the territory of around 85,000 people.

How did Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez respond?

Soon after the call for help from Ceuta, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the government in Madrid was "fully committed to providing an immediate response" to the situation.

"We are mobilizing all necessary resources, working with Moroccan and international authorities, and preparing the necesssary measures to restore normalcy as soon as possible," Sanchez wrote, adding that he had just said as much directly to Vivas.

"This is the moment to build solutions, with responsibility and cooperation," he said, not going into specifics in the post.

Sanchez's Interior Ministry said that the Moroccan government was "closely cooperating" with Spain to handle the situation and that Moroccan police were stopping "numerous people" trying to cross the border. It said that both countries had agreed to work together "for the return, as soon as possible, of all the people who entered Ceuta illegally."

Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska made plans to visit Ceuta on Friday and evaluate the situation, the ministry said.

Why is the rush happening now?

It's not yet clear why large groups are suddenly seeking entry to Ceuta in the past few days, even though a couple of relatively recent developments at least bear a tangential relationship to the issue.

Earlier in July, the Spanish Supreme Court ruled that migrants arriving by sea could not immediately be pushed back across a border in the same way as they could at a land border crossing.

The Ceuta and Melilla enclaves in North Africa bordering Morocco do present exceptional cases where this ruling is concerned, in that it is technically possible to enter them "by sea" despite the fact that you are essentially circumventing a border crossing on land, not crossing the Strait of Gibraltar or the Mediterranean.

One less recent development that attracted international attention, meanwhile, is the Spanish government's offer of amnesty and residency permits to migrants who can demonstrate that they had already entered the country without legal authorization. However, that rule only applies to people who can prove they were already in Spain when it came into force, so it does nothing to improve the prospects of staying for people entering by irregular means now.

Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, at least, drew a parallel between the amnesty and Thursday's events, calling for the EU's open-border Schengen area to be "closed to Spain," and alleging that the amnesty had encouraged human trafficking. 

Tajani's Spanish counterpart, Jose Luis Albares, condemned the Italian minister, saying it was "improper" for "a partner and friendly country from which we expect European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery."

 

Edited by: Sean Sinico

entries.title: Kenya: 15 dead elephants likely poisoned by cyanide
entries.summary: The elephants ate contaminated tomatoes from nearby farms. It was unclear if the poisoning was deliberate or accidental.
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

The elephants ate contaminated tomatoes from nearby farms. It was unclear if the poisoning was deliberate or accidental.

Wildlife officials in Kenya said on Thursday that 15 elephants found dead this month in one of the country's best-known wildlife parks were likely poisoned by cyanide.

Authorities said the poison likely originated from pesticides used on farms. The elephants lived in Amboseli National Park near the Tanzanian border.

Kenya Wildlife Service spokesperson Duncan Juma Wanyama told the AFP news agency that investigators suspect the elephants ate tomatoes contaminated with "very strong pesticides."

Officials say tomatoes were found in the stomachs of several elephants from the same herd. The animals were likely attracted to unripe plants growing on nearby farms, Wanyama added.

Unclear whether poisoning was deliberate

At least one elephant died on a farm after consuming tomatoes, while other elephants traveled towards a water source before dying days later, despite receiving treatment by vets.

Cyanide is "a toxic substance... which is very lethal, very poisonous," Wanyama said, adding that "whenever the elephant consumed it, it affects their lung and the liver."

Officials did not say who they suspected was responsible for the contamination of tomatoes at farms neighboring the Amboseli National Park.

But it all comes as farmers have been suspected of deliberately poisoning elephants in the past, in order to prevent them from eating their crops.

Wildlife officials are investigating whether other farmers in the area use the same chemicals.

Kenya Wildlife Service has warned that such contamination could have wider consequences for livestock that also graze in the area.

"Other than the elephants and the wildlife that may be feeding in those fields, we have the local livestock. We have the goats. We have the cattle that are there. Eventually, if this is truly what is in the system, then we are going to see a bigger impact,” Kenya Wildlife Service Director General Erustus Kanga said.

'Major setback' for conservation

Amboseli National Park is particularly known for its herds of elephants, as well as its breathtaking savannah landscapes, with Mount Kilimanjaro visible across the border in Tanzania.

The International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) charity said the elephant's poisoning was "a major setback" for one of Africa's key elephant populations.

IFAW said the incident highlighted the devastating impact toxic substances can have on wildlife, livestock, people and ecosystems.

"Those responsible must be held fully accountable under the law," IFAW Kenya director Ben Wandago said.

"This tragedy also underscores the urgent need for the strict control and responsible handling of highly toxic substances to prevent them from entering the natural environment," Wandago added.

entries.title: Berlin Pride attack: Are German juvenile courts too lenient?
entries.summary: The Islamist terror attack on Berlin Pride has put the work of juvenile courts into the spotlight. Many argue the 21-year-old perpetrator should have been in prison at the time of the attack.
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

The Islamist terror attack on Berlin Pride has put the work of juvenile courts into the spotlight. Many argue the 21-year-old perpetrator should have been in prison at the time of the attack.

Could the terrorist attack on Berlin's Pride celebrations, allegedly by a 21-year-old Islamist, have been prevented? This question has been the subject of debate driven largely by the fact that the young German man — born in Germany in 2005 to parents of Lebanese origin — had been convicted and released just weeks before the attack.

Abdul Ballout, who drove his car into a crowd in Berlin's Tiergarten park — killing one woman and injuring 31 people, some seriously — had set out last year intending to join the so-called "Islamic State" (IS) terrorist group in Syria. However, he was arrested en route in Lebanon, detained there and subsequently deported to Germany.

Back in Germany, he stood trial on charges of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. He was found guilty and sentenced in mid-May to 22 months in prison, but this sentence was initially suspended. He was released — and attacked Berlin Pride just weeks later. The day after the incident, he was shot dead by police while they were attempting to arrest him.

Juvenile sentencing can be applied to up to 20-year-olds because the brain is still developing at that age

Since then, juvenile criminal law in Germany has been the focus of criticism. Terrorism expert Peter Neumann from King's College London told the news portal T-Online: "This is a real problem. The sentences are too lenient. In my view, juvenile criminal law is sometimes interpreted too broadly. The protection of the public is not given sufficient consideration."

Juvenile criminal law serves special purposes, says Frieder Dünkel, a criminologist and criminal law expert from Greifswald. "It's primarily about education, about the reintegration of the young person," he told DW.

Judges have considerable leeway and can hand out admonitions or prison sentences.

In Germany, a perpetrator is criminally responsible from age 14 and juvenile criminal law applies. From the age of 18, regular criminal law generally applies, with higher minimum sentences. But juvenile criminal law can also be applied to young adults aged 18 to 20 if they show "developmental delays."

"This is because overall, one can still recognize significant developmental potential in 18- to 20-year-olds," Dünkel said.

This is backed by neuroscientific findings, according to Dünkel, showing that the brain areas responsible for behavioral control do not fully develop until the middle of the third decade of life. This implies that a young offender can still change for the better.

In May, Abdul Ballout was sentenced by the Berlin court under juvenile criminal law, even though he was already 21 at the time of his sentencing. However, he was only 20 years old when he committed the crimes he was found guilty of.

'Preliminary probation' for Ballout

Ballout was able to leave the courthouse because he had been granted six months of "preliminary probation," after which the court would have had to make a final decision on whether he needed to go to prison. He was initially placed under intermittent police surveillance until the police officers concluded that he was behaving unobtrusively.

He was ordered to participate in an exit program for extremists, where he attended two preliminary meetings to determine whether he was indeed willing to critically examine his behavior and distance himself from extremism.

Preliminary probation is a relatively new concept in Germany's criminal law and was introduced in 2012. Frieder Dünkel believes that the mechanism has been successful in many cases.

"Specifically, when a juvenile court judge is unsure whether a sentence can or should be suspended in favor of probation, the judge orders a period of up to six months during which the young person is guided toward a law-abiding lifestyle through strict directives and monitoring measures," Dünkel explained.

German interior minister wants to reform juvenile criminal law

In the aftermath of the Berlin Pride attack, there have been calls to stop applying the more lenient juvenile criminal law to Islamist or right-wing extremist perpetrators.

But criminologist Dünkel disagrees: "It is not the role of juvenile criminal law to provide preventive protection for society before a crime has even been committed. Juvenile criminal law responds to crimes once they have been committed," he says.

Juvenile criminal law does allow for severe penalties; for instance, a murder conviction can result in a 15-year prison sentence for offenders aged 18 to 20.

Dünkel adds that recidivism rates among perpetrators sentenced under juvenile criminal law are no higher than among those sentenced under adult criminal law.

"Harsher penalties do not lead to greater security," he said.

Nevertheless, Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) has announced his intention to examine ways to reform juvenile criminal law.

Konstantin von Notz, the opposition Green Party's expert on internal affairs disagrees with that approach. 

"We... note that virtually all experts consulted on this matter so far point out that long prison sentences — especially for young adults — can have a counterproductive effect and may even accelerate existing radicalization," von Notz said.

Information sharing glitch

Ballout had been classified as a dangerous individual by Germany's Joint Counter-Terrorism Center (GTAZ). The GTAZ is a coordination and communication platform established in 2004, after the 9/11 terror attacks in the United States, to combat Islamist terrorism through inter-agency information sharing.

However, the assessment of Ballout did not reach the Berlin court that handed down the lenient sentence earlier this year. If the information had been shared, Ballout may have remained incarcerated.

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Epstein files: How victims remain exposed to identification
entries.summary: US officials vowed to revise redactions after files exposed information that identified survivors of sexual abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and his associates. A DW investigation found that sensitive information remains online.
entries.content:
United States of America

Epstein files: How victims remain exposed to identification

July 30, 2026

US officials vowed to revise redactions after files exposed information that identified survivors of sexual abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and his associates. A DW investigation found that sensitive information remains online.

"I cannot live without looking over my shoulder," a sexual abuse survivor told US lawmakers in May, describing how her personal information was publicly exposed in January, when the Department of Justice (DOJ) released hundreds of thousands of documents related to the financier Jeffrey Epstein. "I can only imagine the long-term impact this mistake will have on my life." 

Three days after the DOJ released the largest of 12 datasets on Epstein on January 30, a department lawyer told a federal court that "human or technical error" had been among the factors that led to the publishing of personally identifying information of people who had been sexually abused by Epstein and his associates. As a result, the DOJ said it would remove, review and redact flagged documents before republishing them.

DW's investigative unit, along with its Innovation and Data teams, spent months reviewing thousands of documents released by the DOJ. In the six months since the release, DW identified dozens of files that still contained information — including names, faces and email addresses — that could be used to identify survivors, witnesses and informants, among other people.  

DOJ Epstein Library

By mid-February, DW had scraped more than 800,000 files from the DOJ's Epstein Library — a challenging task with the archive constantly changing: New files were being added, others were taken down and modified files were popping up after days of absence.

But it wasn't until DW obtained an earlier set of files archived by a publicly facing data preservation project on GitHub that we realized more than 500,000 files were removed between the initial days of the release and our scrape.

To verify the contents of the original release, DW generated a unique digital fingerprint, known as a hash, for every document. Hashes confirm that a document matches the original and hasn't been altered. By comparing these fingerprints with documents scraped from the DOJ website about two weeks later, DW could determine which files matched, as well as identify documents that had been removed from the DOJ website.

DW also found that some files had changed because the digital fingerprint was no longer the same: They had the same file name but were larger or smaller than the original. When DW reviewed this subset, we found that they represented files that had been further redacted — or information was added.

In one instance, a survivor described how Epstein had abused her for years as a minor in her testimony to lawyers. Her name was redacted throughout the transcript until the last page, when a lawyer thanked her for her testimony and said her name, and it remains unredacted as of publication.

Her exposed name was not an isolated case.

Deep audio analysis

To analyze audio files, including victim statements and tipoffs, DW's investigative unit collaborated with the Fraunhofer Institute for Digital Media Technology's Media Distribution and Security research group in Ilmenau, Germany. The MDS specializes in audio authenticity, manipulation and speech synthesis detection.

After removing duplicated files from the publicly facing data preservation project and DW's scrape, we were left with more than 150 audio files, which the MDS's forensic audio researchers analyzed using state-of-the-art tools developed at the institute. They detected digital traces left by audio production and editing processes that are, at times, inaudible to the human ear.

That included identifying parts of a recording that had been modified or reused, determining whether a recording was an altered version of another file, and assessing whether audio files may have been recorded using the same microphone or recording setup.

Forensic audio researcher Milica Gerhardt observed something unique: that redaction styles varied across the files, along with inconsistencies in how redactions were executed.

"If one observes the content of these audio files, one can see that a lot of personal information has not been redacted," Gerhardt said.

In one case, a person called an official tipoff hotline to report information for use in an investigation into Epstein's abuse. In the redacted version, you can hear the person's name, but their phone number was bleeped out.

The same dataset, however, also contained a different version of the audio file, in which the person's full name could be heard as well as their direct contact. Alleged witnesses or informants were apparently not included in the protections allotted to victims.

"They could and should have done a better job on the redactions," said Patrick Aichroth, who heads the MDS group at the Fraunhofer Institute, which has consulted on audio-related evidence for judicial authorities in Germany.

"There is a reason why such material is treated so carefully in court cases," Aichroth said. "Once sensitive or identifying information is disclosed, the damage cannot be undone."

DOJ's redaction failures

DW's investigative unit confronted the DOJ with its findings, including examples in which survivors' personally identifiable information remained in the official Epstein Library.

The DOJ did not respond.

In April, the DOJ's Office of the Inspector General, an independent watchdog tasked with investigating misconduct within the department, announced that it was "initiating an audit of DOJ's compliance with the Epstein Files Transparency Act."

"Our preliminary objective is to evaluate the DOJ's processes for identifying, redacting and releasing records in its possession as required by the Act," the office said in a statement.

In July, several lawmakers introduced the Epstein Files Transparency Act II, which would allow sexual abuse survivors and the governments of US states to take the DOJ to court for failing to comply with the rules laid out in the initial Transparency Act, which had guaranteed that the personally identifiable information of survivors would be protected. 

Survivors whose information was published unredacted have since shared accounts of harassment, humiliation and physical threats. With the publicly disclosed information still available on public platforms and, in some cases, still on the DOJ website, the impact continues to upend survivors' lives.

"While the rich and powerful remain protected by redactions, my name was exposed to the world," said the sexual abuse survivor who gave her testimony to Congress in May.

"The evidence is right here," she said, "yet those in power [would] rather us die socially, emotionally and physically than admit their own complicity."

Edited by: Mathias Bölinger, Milan Gagnon

Technical and data analysis by: Andreas Giefer

Data journalists: Gianna Grün, Rodrigo Menegat Schuinski

Fact checking by: Birgitta Schülke

entries.title: UEFA votes to boycott World Cup over FIFA investor plan
entries.summary: UEFA members unanimously voted to boycott ‌the ⁠World ⁠Cup and other competitions unless FIFA abandons its private investor plans. "The World Cup is not for sale," they said, as FIFA seeks to sell a stake in it.
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

UEFA members unanimously voted to boycott ‌the ⁠World ⁠Cup and other competitions unless FIFA abandons its private investor plans. "The World Cup is not for sale," they said, as FIFA seeks to sell a stake in it.

European football's governing body, UEFA, voted unanimously to boycott FIFA competitions if the world governing body proceeds with plans to create a new commercial subsidiary valued at $20 billion (roughly €17.5 billion) and sell a non-controlling minority stake in it to investors.

The subsidiary would be responsible for FIFA's commercial rights like broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing contracts for its competitions, including the World Cup.

UEFA's 55 members met to discuss a response to FIFA President Gianni Infantino's controversial plans.

"No UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership," UEFA said in a statement.

"The World Cup cannot be treated as an investment product... No part of it should ever be surrendered to private investors. The World Cup is not for sale," the statement added.

Shortly after, North America’s soccer body CONCACAF unanimously rejected the FIFA plan, though it stopped short of a boycott.

UEFA swiftly rejected FIFA's proposal

UEFA had come out publicly in opposition to the plan within an hour of it first being reported by the Financial Times and Times on Tuesday.

Shortly after the newspaper reports, FIFA, the sport's global governing body, issued a statement confirming the plan.

In a later statement, it gave FIFA's 211 member associations until September 19 to express their written support for the scheme. The proposal requires a simple majority and approval from the FIFA Council to pass.

Even before Thursday's meeting, UEFA had doubled down on its criticism after learning of the deadline, saying: "Today we have learned of FIFA's deadline to associations to support their proposals or have the one-off payout offer withdrawn. This says everything ​you need to know about this plan.

It added that talks with many stakeholders showed that "there is significant and growing opposition to FIFA's scheme. FIFA cannot to use our sport to enrich themselves and their friends."

DFB: FIFA plan 'problematic and unacceptable'

Germany's mass-circulation Bild paper reported that key UEFA officials including German FA (DFB) President Bernd Neuendorf had already discussed the FIFA plans via a video call on Wednesday.

"We must not lose the fans' support, but we are well on the way to squandering that," he told public broadcaster ZDF. "I consider this to be extremely problematic and unacceptable.

"If UEFA rejects this request (for approval of the plan), then it is dead, because I believe that you won't be able to find any investor who would be willing to go ahead with this project if UEFA is out," he added.

Other critics have expressed fears that the deal could lead to more tournaments, teams and matches to increase revenue and boost the value of investors' stakes.

UEFA hasn't been the only confederation to criticize the report. CONCACAF, responsible for North and Central America, as well as the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) have also expressed concerns that the proposal was made public without their consultation while the African confederation (CAF) have said they will discuss the plans next week.

Members of the FIFA Council, including Neuendorf, have said they were not consulted on the latest proposal.

FIFA: Subsidiary could raise billions 'this year'

FIFA has said the new subsidiary, to be known as FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) would be valued at $20 billion and that it would aim to raise up to $4.2 billion "this year" by "carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests" in the company.

Under the ​plan, FIFA said it could make $10 billion available for development beginning in 2027. Each federation would be eligible for up to $20 ​million in one-time Fast Forward funding, in addition to $20 million through the regular FIFA Forward program during the 2027-30 ⁠cycle. Without ​approval, FIFA projects a development package of about $2.7 billion.

Infantino: 'A golden opportunity'

In the face of the opposition, FIFA President Gianni Infantino released a video on Wednesday evening, describing the project a "golden opportunity to turbocharge the development of the game globally."

He added that the proposal was "part of a democratic process" and in comments directed to football fans, he stressed that "the sport they watch and love will not change."

Edited by: Matt Pearson

entries.title: EU aims to build AI gigafactories of its own
entries.summary: The EU has unveiled a plan to raise state and private funds to hyperscale AI capabilities and gain independence from non-European governments. The plan calls for the construction of seven new sites across the bloc.
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

The EU has unveiled a plan to raise state and private funds to hyperscale AI capabilities and gain independence from non-European governments. The plan calls for the construction of seven new sites across the bloc.

The European Commission on Thursday announced a call for tenders designed to generate over €30 billion ($34 billion) in state and private funding for the construction of seven so-called AI gigafactories to boost the European Union's computing independence.

Of the funds, €10 billion will come from the EU and member states while private investors put up the remaining €20 billion.

The funds are to be collected and distributed by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU), which was launched in 2020 to develop "a world class supercomputing ecosystem by pooling the resources of the European Union, European countries and private partners."

Consortia and special ⁠purpose ​vehicles (SPVs) made up of technology and ​cloud service providers, public entities and investors are all eligible to apply for funding.

Chipmakers AMD, ​Nvidia and Qualcomm have all signed letters of intent to provide chips to groups involved in the projects, according to the Commission.

The Commission said the scheme will "expand Europe's AI computing capacity and give start-ups, scale-ups, small and medium-sized enterprises, industry, academia and public authorities access to infrastructure."

Speaking of the construction of the facilities — which will produce advanced AI processors, software and cloud technology stacks, high-speed connectivity and energy-efficient data centers — Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission's executive vice-president for Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy, called the moment "a milestone."

"Access to the raw scale of computing power within AI gigafactories is a strategic necessity for Europe as AI development accelerates," she said in a statement.

EU beholden to US and China when it comes to tech

Currently, the EU operates 19 data centers located between Spain and Finland.

The bloc remains heavily reliant upon foreign actors for its tech, however, something that makes it and its member states extremely vulnerable to the whims of outside forces.

US President Donald Trump, for instance, has made clear his intention to leverage American economic heft to influence how the bloc and its members regulate US tech.

For its part, China has limited the supply of minerals critical to the sector.

The EU now hopes to triple data center capacity within five to seven years in order to gain independence but sees challenges when competing with the US and China, where, among other things, energy is far cheaper.

A recent report issued by the European Commission and presented to the EU Parliament was bleak in its outlook should the situation remain as it is, warning, "European businesses and public authorities will continue to rely on US AI providers to the detriment of European service providers struggling to work at the frontier."

"Dependence on hyperscale cloud and AI computing service providers, particularly for highly critical use cases," the report said, "will continue to expose data to third-country access and carry risks to service continuity, endangering operational autonomy."

EU selling tech, are citizens willing to buy?

EU leaders have sounded the alarm over the bloc's lagging efforts on the AI front, yet some citizens are leery of the tech for a host of social, economic and environmental reasons.

The Commission has sought to allay fears with pledges that the new technology will be developed and operated according to "EU standards on data protection, safety, security and ethics," in reference to the bloc's Digital Services Act and  Digital Market Act.

Beyond fears of massive job losses caused by AI, the construction of massive tech facilities has faced global backlash over environmental concerns due to their voracious appetite for water and electricity as well as the inordinate amount of noise pollution they produce.

The European Commission says it will accept bids for its new projects until November 12, and begin distributing funds in early 2027 so that construction can begin within the year.

entries.title: Human trafficking in Mexico: the dark side of tourism
entries.summary: By May, a record-breaking 20 million tourists had visited Mexico so far in 2026. But with increased tourism comes a heightened risk of human trafficking and sexual exploitation. Women and children are most vulnerable.
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

By May, a record-breaking 20 million tourists had visited Mexico so far in 2026. But with increased tourism comes a heightened risk of human trafficking and sexual exploitation. Women and children are most vulnerable.

Warning: This article discusses sexual violence, which some readers might find distressing.

Mixi Cruz was just 13 years old when her mother died. At first, she lived on the streets, then she turned to her elder stepsister for help. Once there, she was forced to manage household chores and pressured into sexual exploitation. 

"The hardest part was accepting that none of that happened simply because I was naive or stupid," the young woman, now 33, tells DW. "It happened to me because there are bad people who sell other people. And there are bad people who buy other people."

In Mexico human trafficking has become one of the most lucrative economies in organized crime. According to the 2025 Global Organized Crime Index by the Swiss-based Global Initiative organization combating transnational organized crime, criminal synidicates are becoming more and more involved. These include the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generacion, CJNG) and the Sinaloa Cartel. 

Within just one year, the number of incidents reported to authorities spiked by 45%.

On World Day Against Trafficking in Persons, July 30, the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) is calling for tighter, cross-border cooperation between judiciaries and law enforcement. Experts say that so far, only a fraction of the actual cases are being reported, let alone solved. 

Perpetrators exploit vulnerabilities

Mixi Cruz was exploited by her own family. She was made to look after five children, and iron laundry until late at night. She still has scars on her hands, from when she'd fall asleep and burn herself with the iron, she says.

Not longer after, she was pressured into sex work for money. She was 14.

Many survivors don't know at the time that they are experiencing sexual violence, she says.

"Many think they're in love, or their own family sells them," Cruz explains. "From the time they're little, they're made to believe violence is normal, and just part of what love is."

In Mexico, the civil-society organization Consejo Ciudadano para la Seguridad y Justicia (Citizens' Council for Security and Justice) estimates that seven out of 10 human trafficking survivors are female. More than half of them are minors.

Hidden human trafficking figure much higher, experts say

"Human trafficking is a game of deceit, it involves a high level of emotional manipulation to isolate victims and prevent them from reaching out and building support networks," Gabriela Gonzalez Garcia explains. She is the director general of citizen services for the Citizens' Council.

Her organization runs Mexico's only specialized 24-hour hotline , as well as a live chat, for people affected by human trafficking. Since it was founded in 2007, the organization has counted some 26,000 cases. But the real number, Gonzalez says, is far higher, likely around 98%. 

Ana Torres and three volunteers are in a red-light district near the edge of Mexico City. She's asked not to be mentioned by her real name. Now in her late 20s, she's been leading a street project for the past five years for El Pozo de Vida ("The Well of Life" in Spanish) that combats human trafficking and sexual exploitation. Each week, Torres and her colleagues visit a different part of Mexico's capital, speaking with the women there and offering help. 

Before this year's soccer World Cup in Mexico, Canada and the United States, many sex workers had hoped for higher earnings, but Torres says the demand remained virtually unchanged. But what did increase noticeably was the number of foreign tourists, and with it, another source of danger for the women on the streets: the language barrier.

"Maybe they reach an agreement (with clients) on the street," Torres explained. "But what really happens when they get a room?"

Raising awareness for human trafficking

The UNODC and its Mexican partners the like Citizens' Council used campaigns like Mundial sin Trata ("A World Cup Without Human Trafficking" in Spanish) to make the tourism industry more aware of the increased risk of human trafficking during the World Cup. A popular driving service joined the campaign, and an online homestay operator teamed up with the UNODC to offer workshops for hosts.

But Cruz says she's skeptical that was enough to curb trafficking and exploitation.

"Men don't pay for sex because they traveled here just for that. They do it because an opportunity presents itself," Cruz said. "In any tourist district, people can tell you where to find prostitution, where you can find women, or children."

'They're locked away and guarded'

In the red-light district, it's starting to rain. Many sex workers have disappeared into nearby houses. A young woman is standing at the corner, wearing black high-heels, a short green dress, grey denim jacket, dark hair to her shoulders. Rain drops bounce off her umbrella. Ana Torres approaches her.

The young woman says she's worried about one of her colleagues, from Colombia, who's currently hiding somewhere in the city. She talks about a family of pimps that targets Colombians, luring them to Mexico with fake promises.

The pimp's wife, she says, has an iron grip on operations: "She makes them work 12 to 15 hours a day, they're not even allowed to eat alone," the woman told DW. "They're locked away and guarded in houses."

Ana Torres asks the woman to pass her organization's number on to her colleague who has fled. The young woman has tears streaming down her face as Ana Torres commends her for her courage to speak up for others.

On the way back, Ana says she's under the impression the pimps and their overseers were watching the women more closely that evening than they usually would. She says she's not quite sure why, but it worries her.

Mixi Cruz was 16 when she finally managed to run away. Today, she's part of a survivors' network that visits schools and universities to raise awareness for human trafficking. Her stepsister was eventually sentenced to four years in prison, her stepsister's husband got five years. In the end, they weren't convicted for human trafficking, but for other serious offenses. But even that is unusual.

This article was translated from German.

If you or someone you know have experienced any kind of gender-based violence, the website lila.help lists trustworthy helplines and NGOs that offer support in almost every country in the world.

entries.title: How crypto miners are stealing power in Southeast Asia
entries.summary: Across Southeast Asia, illegal cryptocurrency miners are stealing vast amounts of electricity, straining national grids and exposing links to organized crime.
entries.content:
July 30, 2026

Across Southeast Asia, illegal cryptocurrency miners are stealing vast amounts of electricity, straining national grids and exposing links to organized crime.

A raid in Malaysia last week exposed how cryptocurrency mining is becoming entangled with electricity theft and organized crime across Southeast Asia.

In Malaysia's southern state of Johor, 71 cryptocurrency-mining machines had been running around the clock across four rented premises for about a month before police moved in.

During the raids on July 22 and 23, officers arrested three suspects and seized computers, routers and vehicles alongside equipment used to illegally mine Bitcoin. 

Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said the syndicate bypassed electricity meters, leading to an estimated €14,500 ($16,600) in losses in about a month, according to local media reports. The machines were thought to be generating between €17,200 and €21,500 in monthly revenue.

The case was relatively small by Malaysian standards. Between 2020 and 2025, national utility Tenaga Nasional Berhad (TNB) identified almost 14,000 premises linked to electricity theft for cryptocurrency mining. Its cumulative losses reached around €1.1 billion.

Detected cases increased from 610 in 2018 to 2,397 in 2024, according to Malaysia's Energy Ministry, which has described illegal mining as a serious threat to public safety, economic stability and the national electricity system.

"In Malaysia, thousands of incidents have triggered investigations into illegal mining for cryptocurrency purposes," said Sonny Zulhuda, an associate professor at the International Islamic University Malaysia.

"This poses a huge problem for the security of electricity resources, economic sustainability, competition and revenue loss," Zulhuda told DW.

"Enforcement has been lagging behind due to a lack of legislative preparedness and limited agency capability in enforcement and investigation. This is unfortunate because Malaysia is fast developing its digital infrastructure."

Where crypto mining meets organized crime

Cryptocurrency mining is not inherently criminal. However, authorities are increasingly finding links between illegal crypto mining, online gambling, money laundering and Southeast Asia's industrial-scale cyber scam networks.

Last October, the United States and the UK sanctioned Cambodia-based Prince Group and associated companies, alleging that the network operated forced-labor scam compounds and laundered proceeds through cryptocurrencies and other assets.

US authorities also seized Bitcoin worth around $15 billion at the time from wallets whose private keys were held by Prince Group chairman Chen Zhi, describing the cryptocurrency as proceeds and instruments of fraud and money laundering.

Thailand's Department of Special Investigation has made the clearest connection between stolen electricity and transnational crime.

In 2025, investigators dismantled three major illegal crypto mining networks, seized more than 6,390 machines and estimated losses to the Provincial Electricity Authority at more than €24.9 million.

In one operation, authorities found around 1,900 mining machines at warehouse sites. The electricity authority estimated that the network was consuming power worth around €575,000 each month while paying only a fraction of the amount due.

Indonesia battles crypto mining crimes as well

Indonesia has seen similar cases. In December 2023, police in the province of North Sumatra raided ten sites and seized more than 1,100 Bitcoin-mining machines. State utility PLN estimated losses over six months at around €700,000.

Governments have responded with raids, tougher penalties and cooperation between police, utilities, regulators and anti-corruption agencies. Malaysia has created a multi-agency committee and deployed smart meters at substations to identify abnormal consumption. 

But enforcement remains difficult. Equipment can be moved quickly, premises can be rented through intermediaries and meter tampering may involve organized networks or insider assistance.

Saaidal Razalli Azzuhri, a telecommunications expert at the University of Malaya, told DW that raids should be supported by transformer-level monitoring, mandatory licensing, disclosure of companies' beneficial owners and investigations tracing bank transfers and cryptocurrency wallets.

"The objective should not be to prohibit blockchain technology, but to ensure that miners pay the full economic cost of their electricity and do not transfer their costs and infrastructure risks to the public," he said.

Zulhuda said that Southeast Asian governments need to deal with this issue properly so they don't send the wrong message to companies that want to invest in the region's growing digital sectors.

Malaysia has several laws to curb illegal cyber activities, including the Cyber Security Act 2024 to protect its National Critical Information Infrastructure and the recently enacted Cybercrimes Act 2026 to address digital system misuse and abuse, he added.

Laos pulls the plug

Laos shows that even legal, state-backed cryptocurrency mining can struggle to deliver the promised benefits.

In mid-2021, the government authorized six companies to mine and trade cryptocurrencies. The plan appeared suited to a country that had invested heavily in hydropower and sometimes produced more electricity than its economy could absorb. Mining offered a way to monetize surplus energy.

At its peak in 2021 and 2022, the industry consumed around 500 megawatts. But the surplus proved unreliable.

Some miners accumulated unpaid bills. More importantly, officials concluded that the industry created few jobs and little demand for domestic suppliers compared with manufacturing or other commercial activities.

Deputy Energy Minister Chanthaboun Soukaloun said last October that the government intended to end electricity supplies to miners.

Laos wants to redirect the power towards metals processing, electric-vehicle manufacturing and artificial intelligence data centers, while increasing electricity exports to neighboring countries.

The experiment offered a broader warning. Cheap electricity can attract crypto miners, but it does not guarantee lasting investment or wider development. When operators steal power, or consume subsidized electricity without creating much value, the public is left carrying the cost.

Edited by: Keith Walker
